title: A read-only window into my lab for AI agents
summary: I gave my coding agents a typed, read-only view of my homelab over MCP, and an independent review agent caught me widening what they could read.

stat.label: the work-item tool refuses any project outside its list, and a test proves it asks the tracker nothing first

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My coding agents work in the cloud and cannot reach my home network, so every question about live state went through me. A general shell tool would have fixed that and handed an agent far more power than it needs. I wanted the agent to see the lab and nothing more.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A Model Context Protocol server that exposes the lab as a small set of typed tools: host lookups, guest state, monitor status, git history, service health and work-item lookups. A model calls a tool with validated input and gets a capped answer that names what it read. There is no shell tool, and a read that fails returns an error with its cause, never an empty success.

Two upgrades make it sharper. The work-item tool now takes a key from any board the server may read and finds the project itself, so an agent no longer needs a hand-fed project identifier. And one overview tool replaces several separate calls for "what is wrong right now". It reads its sources in parallel and returns a short list of what needs a look. Each source succeeds or fails on its own, and a source that cannot be read is named in the list. An unreadable source never counts as healthy.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: An agent can name the work items a commit cites in one call, and see the state of the lab in one call. In live use the server reads one board, PET, so the multi-board path is tested but not yet exercised. I have no measurement of time saved, and I am not claiming one.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: My first version of the work-item tool resolved any project in the workspace. The tests passed. I handed the diff to a fresh review agent and told it nothing about whether the change was safe. It pointed out that I had removed a hard limit. Before, the tool could read one board. Now a model, or text a model had been tricked by, could ask for any board, including one I treat as personal.
I had tested that the code worked and never asked what it could now reach. I added an allowlist of project identifiers, checked before the server contacts the tracker at all.

sections.heading: The tested control
paragraphs: The limit is the allowlist, and tests cover both sides. A key from an allowed board resolves and returns its title and state. A key from a board outside the list is refused, and the test asserts that no work-item request left the server. The refusal means something because the allowed case succeeds beside it. I also ran the refusal against the live server, and it named the allowed boards in its error.
The overview has its own negative cases: a dead source shows up as unread, a source that answers in the wrong shape is reported by name, and a failure of every source fails the call.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: When a change makes a tool more general, ask what it can now reach, and write the refusal as a test.

sources: the lab MCP server's tests, a live check of its refusal, and the review notes
